articles.title: IRS raises 401(k) contribution limits for 2027. Here's how much.
articles.summary: Learn about the 2027 retirement contribution limits and other upcoming 401(k) changes.
articles.body:

If your employer offers a 401(k), you'll be able to save more money for retirement in the new year. The IRS recently announced the new limits for 401(k)s and other tax-advantaged retirement accounts.

The 2027 401(k) contribution limit is $25,500, a $1,000 increase from 2026's limit. If you're 50 or older, you can stash an additional $8,500 in your 401(k). And if you're between the ages of 60 and 63, you can make an even higher extra contribution of $11,750 under the Secure 2.0 Act rules.

The limit on annual contributions to an IRA remains at $7,500.

Read on to learn more about the 401(k) contribution limits for 2027, as well as some new retirement savings rules that should be on your radar.

2026 and 2027 contribution limits for 401(k)s

The IRS adjusts the limits for how much you can save in a tax-advantaged retirement account each year for inflation. It typically does so in increments of $500. Here's a look at how those limits vary across age groups.

There are two main types of 401(k)s: traditional 401(k)s, where you contribute pre-tax money and pay taxes on withdrawals, and Roth 401(k)s, where you've already paid taxes on the contributions and you get tax-free withdrawals in retirement. The contribution limits are the same for both types of 401(k)s.

These limits also apply to several other types of retirement accounts, including:

403(b) plans, which are offered by public schools and some 503(c)(3) tax-exempt organizations

Most 457 plans, which are available to some state and local government employees, as well as employees of some tax-exempt non-governmental entities

The Thrift Savings Plan for federal government employees and uniformed service members

How employer contributions work with 401(k) limits

Many companies match a portion of their employees' contributions to 401(k)s and other retirement accounts. If your employer provides a match, their contribution won't count toward the amount you're allowed to contribute.

However, there are limits on combined employer and employee contributions. In 2026, you and your employer's contributions to your 401(k) can't be more than $72,000, up from $70,000 in 2025.

The $8,000 catch-up contribution that you're allowed to make if you're at least 50 doesn't count toward these limits, nor does the $11,250 catch-up contribution you can make in 2026 if you're between the ages of 60 to 63.

In 2027, the annual limit for combined employer and employee contributions is $75,000.

The $8,500 catch-up contribution that you're allowed to make if you're at least 50 doesn't count toward these limits, nor does the $11,750 catch-up contribution you can make in 2027 if you're between the ages of 60 to 63.

There are no 401(k) income limits; you can contribute to a 401(k) no matter how high your income. But the IRS conducts what's called non-discrimination tests each year to ensure that a retirement plan doesn't disproportionately benefit highly compensated employees. The IRS will consider you a highly compensated employee if:

You own more than 5% of the business at any time during the year or the previous year, regardless of how much you earned, OR

You earned more than $170,000 from your employer in 2026. However, if your employer elects to use the top-paid group rule, you must also rank among the top 20% of employees by compensation.

If you're considered a highly compensated employee, you can still contribute to your 401(k) up to the limits. But if your company's plan fails discrimination testing for a year, it may need to return some of your contributions as a corrective measure.

What is the deadline to contribute to a 401(k)?

You have until the end of the calendar year to make 401(k) contributions, so the deadline for 2026 contributions is Dec. 31, 2026. Any contributions you make after that will count toward the 2027 contribution limits.

Can you contribute to a 401(k) and an IRA?

Yes. You can contribute to both a 401(k) and an IRA as long as you're eligible for each account and stick to the contribution limits. However, if you or your spouse has a 401(k) or any other workplace retirement account, you may be ineligible to deduct contributions to a traditional IRA, or you may only be allowed to deduct a partial amount. Also, keep in mind that income limits apply to Roth IRAs.

New for 2027: Higher retirement contribution limits and changes to income eligibility thresholds

Annual contribution limits for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government's Thrift Savings Plan increased to $25,500, up from $24,500 for 2026.

The catch-up contribution limit for employees aged 50 and older increased to $8,500, up from $8,000, bringing their total potential annual contributions to $34,000. Employees aged 60 through 63 can contribute an additional $11,750 in catch-up contributions in 2027 instead of the standard age-50 catch-up, bringing their total potential annual contributions to $37,250.

The IRS also increased income thresholds for determining eligibility to deduct traditional IRA contributions. For example, the phase-out range for single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan increased to $83,000-$93,000, while the range for married couples filing jointly increased to $133,000-$153,000.

The income thresholds for Roth IRA eligibility also increased for 2027. The income phase-out range for single taxpayers and heads of household will rise to $158,000-$173,000, and for married couples filing jointly, that range will be $250,000-$260,000.

Annual contribution limits for SIMPLE retirement accounts increased to $17,500, up from $17,000 in 2026. Certain eligible SIMPLE plans have a higher limit of $19,100.

The income threshold for mandatory Roth catch-up contributions also increased for 2027. Employees who earned more than $155,000 in FICA wages from the employer sponsoring their retirement plan in 2026 must make any catch-up contributions into a Roth account.

401(k) rules that changed in 2025 and 2026

There are a few new 401(k) rules that took effect in 2025 and 2026, most of which were part of the Secure 2.0 Act. Here are some recent changes that could affect your retirement planning:

Automatic enrollment: Secure 2.0 Act requires 401(k) plans adopted after Dec. 29, 2022, to enroll new employees automatically with a minimum contribution rate of 3%. The plan must also increase the contribution rate by 1% annually, up to at least 10%, but not more than 15%.

Higher catch-up contributions for savers aged 60 to 63: The higher catch-up contribution limits that apply when you're 60 to 63, called super catch-ups, went into effect in 2025.

Part-time worker eligibility for retirement accounts: Beginning in 2025, part-time workers are eligible to participate in the employer's 401(k) or ERISA-covered 401(b) plan after completing 500 hours of service in two consecutive years. The prior requirement was 500 hours in three consecutive years.

Mandatory Roth catch-up contributions for certain high earners: Beginning in 2026, employees who earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages from their current employer in 2025 must make catch-up contributions on a Roth basis. This means contributions are made with after-tax dollars. The requirement applies to eligible employees aged 50 and older.

Roth 401(k)s are no longer subject to RMDs: Required minimum distributions (RMDs) are mandatory distributions you have to take the year you turn 73 (previously 72) from certain retirement accounts. But as of 2024, Roth 401(k)s no longer have RMDs. Traditional 401(k)s are still subject to RMDs.

Annual paper retirement plan statements: Beginning in 2026, 401(k) plans must provide participants with at least one paper benefit statement per year unless they opt into electronic-only delivery.

Will 401(k) contribution limits increase in 2027?

Yes, 401(k) contribution limits are increasing by $1,000 in 2027, to $25,500. The 2026 401(k) contribution limit was $24,500. Catch-up contributions for people 50 and older were $8,000 in 2026 and have increased to $8,500. For the 2026 tax year, people ages 60 to 63 had a higher catch-up contribution limit of up to $11,250, bringing their total potential contributions to $35,750. That limit is increasing to $37,250 in 2027, including the $25,500 standard contribution limit and the $11,750 catch-up contribution.

What percentage of my paycheck should go into my 401(k)?

A good goal to aim for is to save 15% of your pre-tax income in a tax-advantaged retirement account, like a 401(k), 403(b), or IRA. Employer contributions count toward that 15% target. However, if you're getting a late start or want to retire early, you may need to save more since your money has less time to grow.

Maxing out your 401(k) is a smart move when you have a relatively high salary, but it's not necessary or realistic for many people. Aim to contribute at least enough to get your employer's full match, then use your extra money to pay off high-interest debt, like credit cards, and build at least a three- to six-month emergency fund. After that, aim to invest more for retirement by funding an IRA, making unmatched 401(k) contributions, or a combination of both.

articles.title: The AI boom's reliance on circular deals is raising fears of a bubble
articles.summary: AI giants like Nvidia, OpenAI and AMD are investing in one another, raising fears that a weak link could cripple the whole industry.
articles.body: Nvidia plans to invest in OpenAI, which is buying cloud computing from Oracle, which is buying chips from Nvidia, which has a stake in CoreWeave, which is providing artificial intelligence infrastructure to OpenAI. The AI boom that is revolutionizing how people live and work has become increasingly fueled by just a handful of companies turning to one another for the vast amounts of capital and computing power needed to drive their breakneck growth. Some of those partnerships are worth up to hundreds of billions of dollars. Taken together, they have enormously increased the companies’ values, helping send U.S. stock indexes to new highs. But as AI investing grows more insular, there is also a risk that the money flowing between these companies is creating a mirage of growth. If the trend accelerates, some analysts warn, a weak link could threaten the viability of the whole industry — leaving an outsized mark on the U.S. economy. “​​The experience of a quarter of a century ago [when the dot-com bubble burst] won’t necessarily be repeated, but the scale of recent investment increases by tech firms already indicates that they are taking significant risks,” analysts with Oxford Economics research group wrote in a recent note. If it starts to become clear that AI productivity gains — and thus the return on investment — may be limited or delayed, “a sharp correction in tech stocks, with negative knock-ons for the real economy, would be very likely,” they wrote. A web of deals The latest example of that network of investments came Monday, when OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — announced a deal with artificial intelligence chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD. Under the terms of the OpenAI-AMD partnership, OpenAI will purchase AMD’s chips for an undisclosed sum in exchange for the right to take a stake of as much as 10% in the semiconductor giant. The announcement came just weeks after Nvidia unveiled a deal under which it pledged to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI. “Excited to partner with AMD to use their chips to serve our users!” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X. AMD and Nvidia are direct competitors. An Nvidia spokesperson did not immediately respond to an inquiry about whether any OpenAI funds would be used to finance buying its competitor’s chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has characterized his company’s $100 billion OpenAI investment as an opportunity to invest in the next “multitrillion-dollar” company. Nvidia itself is part of that club, with a market valuation of $4.5 trillion. Investments like Nvidia’s in OpenAI are predicated on “the confidence in the revenues” a company can sustain, Huang said on the “BG2” technology podcast. Nvidia and OpenAI already have an indirect collaboration, through the cloud-computing darling CoreWeave, based in New Jersey, which has a standing agreement with OpenAI to sell Nvidia systems to OpenAI. One of CoreWeave’s biggest investors? Nvidia. There are other players in the thicket. Oracle has said it will spend about $40 billion on Nvidia’s chips to power one of OpenAI’s data centers. Oracle and OpenAI are also collaborating with Japan’s SoftBank group on plans to spend $500 billion on additional data centers in a project known as Stargate. Nvidia is a “core technology partner” to the Stargate deal. SoftBank owns a $3 billion stake in Nvidia. An OpenAI representative referred NBC News to CFO Sarah Friar’s recent comments to CNBC, in which she discussed the company’s need for additional computing power. But she did not directly address the “circular” question. Nvidia and CoreWeave declined to comment. Representatives for Oracle and SoftBank did not respond to requests for comment. The doomsday scenario To some investment advisers, the Nvidia-OpenAI deal is especially reminiscent of the ones announced in the lead-up to the 2000 dot-com bubble burst. In March of that year, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index fell by 77% and wiped out billions of dollars in market value. It would take 15 more years before the Nasdaq returned to its March 2000 highs. “There’s a healthy part and an unhealthy part” to the AI ecosystem, said Gil Luria, a managing director at D.A. Davidson financial group who covers technology. The unhealthy part has become marked by “related-party transactions” like the ones involving these companies, he said, which can artificially prop up the value of the firms involved. If investors decide the ties among the AI giants are getting too close, he said, “there will be some deflating activity.” That’s Wall Street-speak for a bubble’s bursting. Altman recently sought to calm fears of a looming AI bust, suggesting that it was part of the life cycle of every industry. “Between the ten years we’ve already been operating and the many decades ahead of us, there will be booms and busts,” Altman said last month during a tour of the massive data center complex that OpenAI is building in Abilene, Texas. “People will over-invest and lose money, and underinvest and lose a lot of revenue," he said. So. Much. Money. Concerns about AI’s insular web of deals and investments have been outweighed by the near-term potential for nearly unimaginable returns. Rather than worry about whether AI is really growing at the pace it appears to be, many investors are instead focused on whether the companies can grow fast enough and make enough profit to justify the mammoth investments being poured into them. “For this whole massive experiment to work without causing large losses, [OpenAI] and its peers now have got to generate huge revenues and profits to pay for all the obligations they are signing up for and at the same time provide a return to its investors,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners and author of The Boock Report. As long as tech-firm valuations keep soaring into the stratosphere and investors keep getting rich, the incentives remain for Wall Street to bless the boom and ignore the doomsday scenarios. As of Wednesday, more than 35% of the market value of all the companies in the S&P 500 Index — more than $20 trillion — came from just seven tech companies, collectively known on Wall Street as the “Magnificent 7.” And each of them — Apple, Google parent Alphabet, Amazon, Facebook parent Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — is heavily involved in AI projects.

articles.title: Alta do dólar: por que o real lidera perdas globais sob Lula? | G1
articles.standfirst: Moeda brasileira sofre pressões tanto do cenário externo como doméstico — onde há indefinição sobre os rumos do ajuste fiscal e sobre quem será o próximo ministro da Fazenda.
articles.summary: A alta do dólar reflete incertezas fiscais no governo Lula e juros nos EUA; analistas projetam que a moeda pode chegar a R$ 6,10 em cenário pessimista.
articles.body:
O real brasileiro foi a moeda, entre as 20 mais usadas no comércio exterior, que mais se desvalorizou no mundo nas últimas semanas — tendo perdido quase 14% do seu valor frente ao dólar americano.

Na segunda-feira, a moeda brasileira teve um novo momento de forte desvalorização. O dólar subiu 2,15% frente ao real e fechou o dia cotado a R$ 5,77 — o maior nível desde abril de 2025.

Um levantamento feito pela BBC News Brasil das cotações, frente ao dólar, das 20 moedas mais usadas no comércio exterior mostra que a desvalorização do real desde 25 de outubro — dia em que foi realizado o segundo turno no Brasil — foi de 13,96%.

Naquele dia, antes de os mercados abrirem após o resultado das eleições, o dólar estava cotado a R$ 4,97 no Brasil.

A perda de valor do real é muito superior a das demais moedas que aparecem na sequência no ranking de desvalorização no período: dólar australiano (desvalorização de 4,25%), dólar da Nova Zelândia (3,54%), coroa norueguesa (3,47%), rand sul-africano (2,17%) e euro (1,99%).

O mais recente boletim Focus (levantamento feito pelo Banco Central) divulgado na segunda-feira mostra que os agentes de mercado esperam que o dólar vai fechar o ano cotado em R$ 5,40 - mas a moeda já está quase 7% acima deste patamar.

Mas as expectativas do mercado vêm se deteriorando. Há quatro semanas, o levantamento mostrava uma projeção de que o dólar terminaria o ano cotado a R$ 5,13.

O movimento de desvalorização do real nas últimas semanas acompanha uma tendência de alta do dólar nos mercados globais — apesar de a moeda brasileira ter um movimento de depreciação mais intenso.

O levantamento da BBC News Brasil mostra que desde o final de outubro apenas três moedas tiveram valorização frente ao dólar: o yuan chinês (0,10%), o peso mexicano (1,12%) e a rúpia indiana (1,59%).

Das 20 moedas mais usadas no comércio exterior, 17 perderam valor frente ao dólar desde o fim de outubro. Desde o começo do ano, foram apenas quatro moedas que se valorizaram diante o dólar. Desde 1º de janeiro, o real foi a sétima moeda que mais se desvalorizou no mundo.

Real foi a moeda que mais desvalorizou — Foto: BBC

Na segunda-feira, houve mais desvalorização de moedas e queda nas bolsas nos principais mercados. O índice Ibovespa, do mercado brasileiro, caiu 1,83% e o Dow Jones, de Nova York, fechou com baixa de 1,41%.

Analistas apontam que existe um movimento de investidores de saída de diversos mercados mundiais em direção aos Estados Unidos — com as perspectivas de os juros americanos virem a subir, à medida que a inflação segue alta na maior economia do mundo.

Muitos consideram que haverá um aumento de juros nos EUA no próximo mês e declarações recentes de autoridades monetárias americanas reforçaram essas expectativas.

Além disso, os mercados atravessam um momento de maior volatilidade, com queda das ações das empresas ligadas à inteligência artificial desde o começo da crise envolvendo a direção da fabricante de chips Nvidia.

"O principal foco das atenções está relacionado à inteligência artificial por uma combinação de fatores", disse Ricardo França, analista de Research da Ágora Investimentos, em transmissão realizada na segunda-feira para analisar o fechamento dos mercados.

"O fato é que as ações de semicondutores, elas continuam em um processo corretivo que já observamos na semana passada. O setor de semicondutores de maneira consolidada está caindo hoje 4,5%, sendo ele responsável por esse movimento de aversão a risco que acaba penalizando o setor de tecnologia, mas se espalha também em outros segmentos."

No Brasil, analistas também apontam as indefinições sobre a economia no próximo governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva — como quem será o próximo ministro da Fazenda e como será o ajuste fiscal.

A proposta de ajuste fiscal apresentada pela equipe econômica na última semana desagradou alguns setores do mercado.

Analistas de bancos e instituições financeiras consideraram as medidas insuficientes para reduzir de forma contínua o ritmo de aumento das despesas e reequilibrar as contas do governo.

"Em nossa visão, as propostas contribuem para um ajuste no curto prazo, mas não resolvem a tendência de crescimento estrutural da dívida pública e deterioração fiscal", escreveu em relatório enviado a clientes Rachel de Sá, estrategista do Research XP, área de análise e pesquisa da XP Investimentos.

Na outra ponta, grupos da esquerda atacaram a iniciativa dizendo que ela atendia a interesses do mercado financeiro e defenderam foco maior na arrecadação. Foram diversas as manifestações nas redes sociais e até na própria base do governo.

O Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) 299/2026 do ajuste fiscal prevê medidas nas duas pontas, para reduzir despesas e aumentar receitas, com uma estimativa de impacto entre R$ 43 bilhões e R$ 54 bilhões, e integra o esforço da equipe econômica para que o resultado primário (a diferença entre arrecadação e despesas, sem contabilizar os gastos financeiros, como pagamento de juros da dívida) seja superavitário em 2027.

A votação no Senado, que começou na última quinta-feira (12/11), deve ser concluída nesta terça (17/11), passando depois à Câmara dos Deputados.

As definições sobre o ajuste fiscal devem ter impacto no câmbio

Em relatório deste mês, a corretora XP afirmou que "depois de se mostrar resiliente durante boa parte de 2026, o real voltou a se depreciar no fim de outubro" e fez diferentes projeções sobre os rumos da moeda brasileira: no cenário mais otimista a moeda ficaria cotada a R$ 4,80; no mais pessimista, perto de R$ 6,10.

O cenário mais pessimista da XP prevê juros americanos em patamar alto e, no Brasil, "uma expansão fiscal sem medidas compensatórias piora a trajetória esperada da dívida pública".

No cenário otimista, a inflação americana cederia, com queda dos juros nos EUA. E no Brasil, "medidas fiscais permanentes" tornariam "mais provável a estabilização da dívida pública".

"Com atividade mais fraca e melhora das expectativas de inflação, o Banco Central retoma o ciclo de cortes de juros", afirma a XP, projetando um câmbio de R$ 4,80 nessa situação.

Segundo o relatório, o futuro do real dependerá em parte das medidas tomadas pelo governo Lula.

"Do lado doméstico, a credibilidade fiscal será importante para a direção da taxa de câmbio. Em 2023, o novo arcabouço fiscal ajudou a reduzir o prêmio de risco e os juros longos", diz o texto.

"Uma melhora semelhante poderia levar o câmbio a R$ 5,20 por dólar ao fim de 2027, se os determinantes do modelo evoluírem conforme nossas hipóteses. O inverso também se aplica: se o ajuste fiscal ficar aquém do esperado, a moeda pode se desvalorizar além dos níveis atuais."

articles.title: PIB do Amazonas cresce 5,6% e tem 4ª maior alta do país, diz IBGE | G1
articles.standfirst: Economia do estado movimentou R$ 177,2 bilhões em 2024, acima da média nacional, de 3,4%. Dados divulgados em novembro de 2026 também revelam que Amazonas manteve a 16ª posição entre as maiores economias brasileiras.
articles.summary: O PIB do Amazonas cresceu 5,6% em 2024, somando R$ 177,2 bilhões com destaque para o Polo Industrial de Manaus e a recuperação da agropecuária após a seca.
articles.body:
PIB do Amazonas cresce 5,6% em 2024 e tem 4ª maior alta do país, aponta IBGE. — Foto: Foto: Bruno Leão/ Sedecti-AM

O Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Amazonas cresceu 5,6% em 2024, em comparação com o ano anterior, e registrou a quarta maior expansão entre os estados brasileiros. Os dados consolidados foram divulgados em novembro de 2026 e mostram que a economia amazonense movimentou R$ 177,2 bilhões no período, acima da média nacional, que foi de 3,4% .

Com o resultado, o Amazonas manteve a 16ª posição entre as maiores economias do país e respondeu por 1,5% do PIB brasileiro . Na Região Norte, o estado permaneceu como a segunda maior economia, atrás apenas do Pará, que registrou R$ 291,1 bilhões .

Em 2023, o PIB amazonense havia alcançado R$ 161,7 bilhões , com crescimento de 2,1% no volume de produção .

Serviços e indústria concentram maior parte da economia

O setor de Serviços teve a maior participação no PIB estadual, com R$ 81,9 bilhões em 2024 . No ano anterior, o segmento havia movimentado R$ 74,9 bilhões .

A Indústria também apresentou crescimento e alcançou R$ 58,8 bilhões , contra R$ 55,1 bilhões em 2023. Dentro do setor, o destaque foi a Indústria de Transformação, que movimentou R$ 46,9 bilhões , o equivalente a 79,7% da atividade industrial e 26,5% de toda a economia do estado .

Segundo a Secretaria de Estado de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (Sedecti), o resultado foi impulsionado pela demanda por produtos fabricados no Polo Industrial de Manaus (PIM). O segmento registrou crescimento de 3,5% no volume de produção.

Já a Agropecuária movimentou R$ 9,3 bilhões em 2024 , ante R$ 7,4 bilhões no ano anterior. Em volume de produção, o setor teve expansão de 19,2% , indicando recuperação após as perdas provocadas pela seca no período anterior.

Amazonas é a segunda maior economia do Norte

Considerando o Valor Adicionado Bruto (VAB), que representa a contribuição dos setores à economia sem incluir os impostos, os Serviços responderam por 54,6% da produção estadual . A Indústria representou 39,2% , enquanto a Agropecuária ficou com 6,2% .

O secretário de Estado de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação, Gustavo Igrejas, avaliou que o desempenho demonstra a recuperação da economia amazonense e destacou a contribuição do Polo Industrial de Manaus.

Segundo ele, os resultados da Indústria de Transformação e da Agropecuária indicam perspectivas positivas para os indicadores econômicos de 2025 e 2026.

O Produto Interno Bruto representa a soma de todos os bens e serviços finais produzidos em uma região durante determinado período.

O cálculo segue o Sistema de Contas Nacionais do Brasil, coordenado pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE), conforme recomendações internacionais da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU).

Os dados consolidados são divulgados com uma defasagem de dois anos devido à complexidade dos levantamentos sobre produção, consumo, comércio, serviços e indústria. Por isso, em 2026, foram apresentados os resultados referentes a 2024.

No Amazonas, a coleta das informações conta com o apoio da Secretaria Executiva de Planejamento (Seplan), vinculada à Sedecti.

articles.title: Durigan diz que reforma tributária pode ter 'pequeno impacto' na inflação e defende reduzir tributos sobre a folha de pagamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro da Fazenda participou de audiência pública na Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos (CAE) do Senado. Segundo ele, a redução dos encargos sobre a folha pode estimular a geração de empregos, desde que não prejudique a Previdência.
articles.summary: Ministro da Fazenda participou de audiência pública na Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos (CAE) do Senado.
articles.body:
Dario Durigan em audiência Pública no Senado Federal — Foto: Washington Costa/MF

O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, admitiu nesta terça-feira (17) que a reforma tributária sobre o consumo, que começa a entrar em vigor em janeiro com a implementação do novo imposto federal, pode gerar um "pequeno impacto" na inflação.

Durante audiência pública na Comissão de Assuntos Econômicos (CAE) do Senado Federal, ele explicou que esse possível impacto está relacionado à implementação do sistema não cumulativo, já adotado em grande parte do mundo.

Isso significa que o imposto será recolhido em cada etapa da cadeia produtiva, mas as empresas poderão abater os valores pagos nas etapas anteriores.

"Pode ter um pequeno impacto na inflação. Estamos passando por um processo em que os empresários vão aprender a precificar, considerando o que há de crédito e débito de sua responsabilidade a ser feito. Ao entender bem essa precificação, vamos ter redução do impacto inflacionário, mas vamos seguir acompanhando isso de perto no Ministério da Fazenda", declarou o ministro a jornalistas.

Aos senadores, Durigan também defendeu a redução da tributação sobre a folha de pagamentos, considerada elevada no país, para estimular a geração de empregos em um eventual quarto mandato do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, "sem que isso cause um prejuízo grande para nossa previdência”.

A proposta foi apresentada mesmo sem a confirmação de que o ministro continuará à frente da Fazenda em 2027.

Atualmente, a contribuição patronal sobre a folha de pagamentos é de 20%. Além disso, os empregadores precisam recolher contribuições para o seguro contra acidentes de trabalho, o FGTS (equivalente a 8% do salário do trabalhador), o salário-educação e o Sistema S.

O empregado, por sua vez, também contribui para a Previdência Social. Somadas, as contribuições de empregadores e trabalhadores variam de 34% a quase 43% no Brasil, segundo os percentuais apresentados no texto. Empresas do Simples Nacional seguem regras diferenciadas de tributação.

“Com relação a desoneração da folha, eu tenho defendido que nós devemos passar, no próximo governo a partir de janeiro do ano que vem, por uma grande reforma ou um processo de reforma da tributação corporativa. Que passa sim por desonerar a folha de pagamento, não só pelas questões nacionais, como o fim da escala 6x1 e a nova escala de trabalho no Brasil", disse o ministro da Fazenda.

Ele também citou a "nova tendência do mundo" de incorporar tecnologias que, em alguns casos, reduzem a necessidade de mão de obra.

"O que me parece do ponto de vista do desenho, do estímulo, vamos estimular a geração de trabalho. Então é importante desonerar a folha, agora sem que isso cause um prejuízo grande para nossa previdência”, acrescentou Durigan.

O ministro também afirmou que a desoneração da folha de pagamentos pode seguir o princípio da "progressividade", pelo qual quem tem maior capacidade financeira paga proporcionalmente mais impostos.

Como exemplo, citou a ampliação da isenção do Imposto de Renda para quem ganha até R$ 5 mil por mês, acompanhada de uma tributação mínima sobre rendas mais altas, acima de R$ 600 mil por ano.

“Nesse processo de desonerar a folha e atribuir, com total compromisso de neutralidade fiscal, essa tributação que incide hoje sobre a folha a outros momentos, seja faturamento ou seja resultado, agregando outros debates. Um debate de mais escadinhas para garantir proporcionalidade e progressividade na tribulação corporativa é bem-vindo”, disse o ministro.

articles.title: Com medidas do governo, projeções apontam que Saúde pode deixar de receber até R$ 9 bi em 2027; Planejamento nega perdas | G1
articles.standfirst: Além da redução de recursos para a área de Saúde, o pacote também prevê redução de benefícios fiscais e do aproveitamento de créditos pelas empresas — medidas que ampliam a arrecadação, o que, segundo o governo, evitaria perdas à saúde.
articles.summary: Além da redução de recursos para a área de Saúde, o pacote também prevê redução de benefícios fiscais e do aproveitamento de créditos pelas empresas — medidas que ampliam a arrecadação, o que, segundo o governo, evitaria perdas à saúde.
articles.body:
A Saúde pode deixar de receber cerca de R$ 9 bilhões em 2027 por conta de medidas do governo, incluindo as que estão previstas no pacote fiscal que está sendo analisado pelo Congresso Nacional.

O cálculo foi feito por Felipe Salto, economista-chefe e sócio da Warren Investimentos , ex-diretor-executivo da Instituição Fiscal Independente (IFI) e ex-secretário de Fazenda do estado de São Paulo (SP).

Já a Consultoria de Orçamentos, Fiscalização e Controle do Senado Federal confirmou um impacto de R$ 6,8 bilhões, por mudanças propostas pelo governo em agosto.

"Mantida a interpretação adotada no projeto de lei orçamentária para 2027, essa exclusão também reduziria a base de cálculo do mínimo da saúde: cada R$ 10 bilhões de arrecadação desse imposto [de exportação, que está vigente em 2026] corresponderiam a R$ 1,5 bilhão a menos no mínimo ", acrescentou a Consultoria, em nota, sobre a retirada do imposto de exportação do cálculo do piso.

A expectativa é de que a votação do texto seja concluída nesta terça-feira (17) pelos senadores. Além da redução de recursos para a área de Saúde, o pacote também prevê a redução de benefícios fiscais e a limitação do aproveitamento de créditos pelas empresas — alterações que ampliam a arrecadação.

Após a publicação da reportagem, o Ministério do Planejamento entrou em contato com o g1 e informou que, com a limitação das compensações de crédito tributário e o corte linear de renúncias fiscais, a arrecadação sobe e a estimativa é que isso eleve os investimentos em saúde em R$ 5 a R$ 6 bilhões.

"Então na verdade o efeito do Projeto de Lei sobre a Saúde é positivo, o Projeto de Lei aumenta a despesa de Saúde, então aquilo que gira em torno de R$ 18 bilhões de reais de crescimento da Saúde para o ano que vem, deve girar em torno de R$ 24 a R$ 25 bilhões de reais se esse projeto for aprovado", disse o Ministério do Planejamento.

➡️ Em agosto, o governo incorporou ao orçamento um gatilho que determina que, no caso de déficit primário neste ano, as receitas da União com a venda de petróleo e gás natural não sejam incluídas no cálculo da chamada "receita corrente líquida" do governo — regra que já foi aplicada no valor previsto para 2027.

➡️ O problema é que o piso constitucional de aplicação da União em Ações e Serviços Públicos de Saúde é justamente 15% da receita corrente líquida, que terá alta menor nos próximos anos com a imposição da regra proposta pela equipe econômica, impondo perda de recursos frente à regra anterior.

➡️ O pacote fiscal, enviado na semana passada ao Congresso, propõe que essas receitas com petróleo não sejam incluídas no cálculo da chamada "receita corrente líquida" do governo até 2030, independentemente de haver déficit ou superávit no ano anterior.

➡️ Além disso, o pacote fiscal avaliado no Legislativo também exclui a receita do imposto de exportação sobre petróleo da conta da receita líquida, o que representará menos recursos caso esse imposto seja mantido.

➡️ Não há estimativas consolidadas sobre o impacto acumulado até 2030. Mas, com a manutenção das novas regras, a saúde deverá receber menos recursos do que receberia pelas regras anteriores, com efeitos ano a ano sobre o crescimento do piso constitucional. Ainda assim, o valor previsto para a saúde em 2027, já considerando a nova regra, é maior do que o destinado à área em 2026 ( veja abaixo ).

De acordo com a Consultoria de Orçamentos do Senado, o governo considerou, na elaboração do orçamento de 2027, que o cálculo do mínimo de aplicação em ações e serviços públicos de saúde a receita corrente líquida seria de R$ 1,81 trilhão, resultando em um mínimo de R$ 272,2 bilhões para a área.

Sem a exclusão, o valor seria R$ 279 bilhões , ou seja, R$ 6,8 bilhões a mais. No comparativo com 2026, entretanto, a destinação de recursos, se confirmada após a aprovação do Orçamento, será maior.

Além disso, a cada R$ 10 bilhões de arrecadação do imposto de exportação, há um adicional de R$ 1,5 bilhão a menos para o piso da Saúde, estima a Consultoria.

Felipe Salto, sócio da Warren Investimentos, informou, em comunicado, que as receitas do petróleo que deixarão de ser consideradas para o cálculo da receita corrente líquida estão estimadas em cerca de R$ 60 bilhões em 2027.

"Pelos meus números. Assim, como o piso da saúde equivale a 15% da RCL [receita corrente líquida], o efeito fiscal seria de R$ 9 bilhões", disse o economista.

Estimativa das medidas da Consultoria Warren Rena — Foto: Consultoria Warren Rena

O ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, estimou que, mesmo com a exclusão das receitas de petróleo do cálculo da receita corrente líquida, o orçamento da área de saúde irá crescer R$ 18 bilhões em 2027. Sem essa medida, portanto, as dotações cresceriam mais ainda.

"No fundo, estamos fazendo algo bem razoável, que é retirar as receitas extraordinárias em relação ao óleo do cômputo do piso de saúde e aí, de novo, se trata de uma racionalização de despesa", afirmou Moretti em audiência pública na Comissão Mista de Orçamento, na semana passada.

Em 2024, o governo avaliou que o envelhecimento da população brasileira eleva pressão por recursos para os serviços de saúde em R$ 67,2 bilhões até 2034 . De acordo com o Tesouro Nacional, essa estimativa toma como base as necessidades de recursos em duas áreas de despesas do orçamento: Assistência farmacêutica, inclusive o programa Farmácia Popular e Atenção de Média e Alta Complexidade — que compreende atendimentos hospitalares e ambulatoriais.

No ano passado, estudo da Instituição Fiscal Independente (IFI), órgão ligado ao Senado Federal, concluiu que o Brasil possui "'crônico subfinanciamento" do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) na comparação com os países mais ricos — que formam a Organização para a Cooperação e Desenvolvimento Econômico (OCDE).

Em nota, o Conselho Nacional de Saúde (CNS), que conta com representantes de usuários do SUS e movimentos sociais, de trabalhadores da área, de secretários de Saúde e até mesmo do governo, criticou a proposta do governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

"O Controle Social do SUS tem, em sua trajetória histórica, a defesa intransigente do Piso Constitucional da Saúde inscrito em nossa Carta Magna. Esse piso não é uma formalidade orçamentária: é a garantia material do direito à saúde, conquistada pela mobilização social e pela luta do movimento sanitário brasileiro", diz o CNS.

Avalia que a flexibilização do piso de saúde, proposta pela equipe econômica, "ainda que sob o argumento da responsabilidade fiscal, significa menos recursos para a atenção básica, para a vigilância em saúde, para a assistência hospitalar, assistência farmacêutica e para o trabalho dos profissionais que sustentam o Sistema Único de Saúde no cotidiano de milhões de brasileiros".

"Alertamos que o ajuste fiscal promovido por meio da diminuição de gastos e investimentos sociais — em especial na área da saúde — foi rechaçado nas últimas eleições presidenciais. O sentimento popular expresso nas urnas foi claro quanto à prioridade do social e do SUS. Parlamentares e o governo eleito devem convergir com esse sentimento, e não com a lógica que trata o direito à saúde como despesa a ser contida", conclui o Conselho Nacional de Saúde.

De acordo com Alessandra Cardoso, assessora política do Instituto de Estudos Socioeconômicos (Inesc), uma organização não governamental brasileira que analisa o orçamento público, retirar as receitas de petróleo do cálculo das receitas correntes líquidas é um grande equívoco, pois vai na contramão dos esforços de ampliar espaço fiscal para políticas sociais essenciais, como é o caso da saúde.

"Para nós, uma trajetória de superação da dependência econômico-fiscal do petróleo exige utilizar esse recurso [do imposto de exportação sobre o produto], juntamente as outras formas de renda, para ampliação do espaço fiscal e financiamento de políticas públicas (...) A medida reforça a lógica de contenção: receitas adicionais não se convertem em maior capacidade de financiar despesas públicas", disse Alessandra Cardoso, do Inesc.

Fachada do Ministério da Saúde. — Foto: Walterson Rosa/MS

articles.title: Trump approval holding near record low of presidency: Survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating is holding close to the lowest point in his presidency, according to a survey released Monday. The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s approval rating sitting at 32 percent. The result has remained the same in the last four surveys released by the polling partners since last month, when his approval rating…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating is holding close to the lowest point in his presidency, according to a survey released Monday.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s approval rating sitting at 32 percent. The result has remained the same in the last four surveys released by the polling partners since last month, when his approval rating notched down to 31 percent, the lowest point of both of his terms.

The survey shows that 66 percent of Americans do not approve of his job performance as president, 2 points down from when his approval rating hit its lowest point.

Support for his agenda also saw a widespread decline over the summer , dipping between the mid to low 30s across several surveys. Americans have soured on the president’s handling of the economy amid concerns over the rising cost of living.

The public has also opposed the Iran war, which contributed to inflation and sent gas prices soaring to an average of almost $5 a gallon, while some states like California have seen averages close to $7 per gallon. Prices have ticked down in recent weeks, with Tuesday seeing the national average hit $3.78 per gallon, a more than 50-cent drop from last month’s average of $4.31 per gallon, according to AAA .

The travel agency stated Monday that less people could be hitting the road or taking flights this upcoming Thanksgiving holiday as a result of the higher price of gas and airfare. An estimated 72.9 million people are expected to travel by car, down from 73.1 million last year.

The Middle East conflict has also been cited by Trump and Vice President Vance as a likely contributor to sweeping Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections earlier this month.

The president has signaled that he would not escalate the conflict after recent negotiations helped lower the steep price of gas, but some experts have said the prolonged uncertainty over the war has extended these high prices.

The president has also touted the U.S.’s military strength over Iran’s since the early days of the conflict, saying last week that the war was “ effectively over ” and that the U.S. “won,” though the massive U.S. military presence in the region remains intact.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey was conducted Nov. 13-16 and included 1,521 respondents. The margin of error is 3 percentage points.

articles.title: "La Inteligencia Artificial y las nuevas tecnologías deben servir al deporte, no al revés"
articles.standfirst: Esteban Granero, Raúl Chapado, Lalo García y Miquel Mir procuran aplicar al rendimiento los datos y las nuevas experiencias... aunque "cualquier decisión seguirán tomándola personas"
articles.summary: Esteban Granero, Raúl Chapado, Lalo García y Miquel Mir procuran aplicar al rendimiento los datos y las nuevas experiencias... aunque "cualquier decisión seguirán tomándola personas"
articles.body: La Inteligencia Artificial está transformando la sociedad. Y, por supuesto, el deporte no es ajeno a la revolución. A partir de los datos y de las nuevas experiencias se están abriendo escenarios inimaginables hace unos años, que fueron analizados en la mesa 'Del atleta aumentado al deporte conectado', moderada por Andrés García, de MARCA. Esteban Granero, CEO de Plexus Sport, exjugador entre otros equipos del Real Madrid, se refería precisamente a su etapa de corto: "Yo he vivido el gran cambio. Cuando empecé mi carrera no existían los datos como materia prima para trabajar con ellos. Todo era arcaico. Cuando me retiré ya había explotado el 'big data' y estábamos inundados de información, pero con poco conocimiento de qué hacer con ella. Ahora se trata de darle sentido para que esas nuevas tecnologías sirvan a las necesidades del deporte, no al revés, porque el interés principal siempre es mejorar, competir y ganar. Lo que no se puede es tratar de imponer algo porque haya funcionado en otros sectores. El deporte es peculiar desde su factor humano". Raúl Chapado introdujo en la Federación Española de Atletismo que preside una plataforma de IA: "Hace siete años ya nos fuimos dando cuenta de la importancia que iba a tener. Te metes en un mundo desconocido, pero empiezas la carrera un poco antes. Hace dos años y medio hubo un punto de inflexión con los fondos que llegaron de la Unión Europea como oportunidad para que las federaciones presentáramos proyectos. El problema era hasta qué punto la tecnología podía ser fiable, porque una milésima o un centímetro te hace luchar por las medallas o te deja fuera. ¿En qué momento estamos? Estamos en el momento de preguntar a la IA en qué momento estamos..." Lalo García, CEO de HubIn (Hub Innovación) y fundador de Celtalab, insistió en una idea: "Tenemos que entender qué necesitan los deportistas para mejorar y tratar de darles herramientas para ello. La IA nos ha permitido trabajar los datos de forma más económica y accesible. Vemos lo que hay fuera, pero también, respecto a la cantera, vemos cómo trabajar con lo que ya tenemos. Trabajamos en distintos ámbitos: físico en cuanto a entrenamiento, competición y recuperación y descanso, pero también psicológico. Cualquier decisión seguirá tomándola una persona... pero con más datos". Miquel Mir es el director comercial Broadcast & Alliances de Cellnex, que se encarga de la conectividad: "La IA es el cerebro, pero es necesario un sistema nervioso que interconecte y dé sentido. Nos hemos convertido en usuarios de nuestro móvil y no somos conscientes de que tenemos cobertura gracias a las importantes inversiones que se han hecho. En los recintos deportivos sucede que decenas de miles de personas intentan acceder de forma simultánea, y para eso es necesario desplegar infraestructuras específicas". Granero completó el panel: "El mercado es lo más importante... y por eso es donde más incidimos. Acertar con los fichajes mueve la balanza financiera y tiene impacto en el rendimiento deportivo. Queremos ayudar para que los clubes tomen las mejores decisiones, reduciendo la incertidumbre. Antes el rendimiento se basaba en las estrellitas que te ponía el MARCA. Tres... y a veces incluso cuatro. Los jugadores siempre pensábamos en qué se basaba esa subjetividad, aunque sabíamos que se trataba de expertos. La tecnología también ha llegado para ayudar en eso, para traer cierta objetividad al rendimiento".

articles.title: American shoppers are taking a breather ahead of the holiday season
articles.summary: Americans reined in some purchases last month – particularly the more expensive items such as cars and furniture – logging the weakest retail sales gain in three months, new data showed Tuesday.
articles.body: Americans reined in some purchases last month – particularly the more expensive items such as cars and furniture – logging the weakest retail sales gain in three months, new data showed Tuesday. US retail sales rose 0.2% in October, a slowdown after gas prices drove a 0.8% gain the month before, according to Commerce Department data. Economists say the overall pullback, however, masks underlying strength of a resilient American consumer who also very well could be gearing up for the holiday shopping season. “The US consumer looks solid and is bending, not breaking, under the weight of higher energy prices,” Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, told CNN. “We know that higher inflation is hurting consumers, but I think that’s just been offset by the strengthening in the labor market we’ve seen this year.” October’s spending tally was driven lower by a drop in car sales that offset a more modest uptick in gasoline station sales (which slowed to a gain of 1.5% versus a 6% increase in September as fuel prices softened a bit after surging higher the two months prior). Retail sales are adjusted for seasonal swings but not inflation, which rose 0.4% in October, Consumer Price Index data shows. Big-ticket purchases drop off In addition to falling sales of cars, Tuesday report showed consumers spent less on furniture, sporting goods and apparel; and also cut back on their purchases at the grocery store. “Conversely, grocery sales declined, which in a nominal report reflects a notable pullback in volume as food inflation outpaces spending,” said Mike Reid, head of US economics for RBC. “But, the weakness there is overshadowed by the strength elsewhere, as upper income households continue to drive consumption.” The pullback on bigger-ticket purchases in October could be an indication that consumers are gearing up for the holiday shopping season, said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. “Several of the categories where spending declined are discretionary categories – purchases you can put off for a while because you don’t need those goods every single month,” she wrote in a note Tuesday. “Because this is October data, savvy families may be saving those purchases for holiday sale deals.” To be sure, a closely watched category of spending that strips out some more volatile areas (such as gasoline stations, auto sales, building materials and restaurants) rose at a stronger-than-expected rate of 0.6%, a tick higher than a 0.5% gain notched in September. Sales at miscellaneous stores (a catch-all category that includes retailers in pet supplies, office goods, florists, Halloween costumes, etc.) saw the biggest gains in October, at 4.7%, while spending remained firm at health and personal care stores as well as online retailers (Amazon, for example, held a sales event early last month). A tale of two consumers Tuesday’s report underscored the ongoing bifurcation of household finances, ING chief international economist James Knightley said, noting the differing trajectories of spending among high-income individuals versus middle- and lower-income Americans. “Middle- and lower-income households tend to spend more of their income of physical goods, such as food and clothing, and squeezed spending power limits the potential for growth,” he wrote. “Conversely, high income households have seen their wealth surge, boosting consumption, and are accounting for a growing share of total consumer spending.” In addition to Tuesday’s retail sales data, a fuller picture of consumer health and spending could come via Target and Walmart, which are slated to release their latest earnings reports on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, this week. Consumers appear to still have an appetite to spend but are being picky about what they’re buying, EY-Parthenon economists wrote Tuesday. “Cost-of-living concerns were front and center in the midterm elections and underscored the lasting imprint of accumulated inflation on household finances,” wrote economists Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour. “While consumers still have the capacity to spend, it should not be confused with comfort.”

articles.title: SELLAS Life Sciences stock soars 240% on positive cancer trial
articles.summary: Investing.com -- SELLAS Life Sciences Group (NASDAQ:SLS) shares surged 240% after the company announced positive topline results from its pivotal Phase 3 REG...
articles.body:
Investing.com -- SELLAS Life Sciences Group (NASDAQ:SLS) shares surged 240% after the company announced positive topline results from its pivotal Phase 3 REGAL trial of galinpepimut-S (GPS), an immunotherapeutic cancer vaccine for acute myeloid leukemia.

The REGAL trial met its primary endpoint of overall survival, with GPS demonstrating a 41% reduction in the risk of death compared to best available treatment. The trial showed a median overall survival of 24.0 months for GPS-treated patients versus 14.7 months for the control group, with a hazard ratio of 0.59 and a two-sided p-value of 0.035.

The trial evaluated GPS as maintenance monotherapy in patients with acute myeloid leukemia who achieved a second or later complete remission following second- or later-line salvage therapy and who were ineligible for, or unable to undergo, allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

GPS was generally well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with prior clinical experience and no new safety signals identified. Treatment-related adverse events were predominantly mild to moderate, most commonly consisting of local injection site reactions.

The topline primary endpoint data analysis was conducted following the pre-specified occurrence of 80 events in accordance with the trial's pre-specified statistical analysis plan. SELLAS plans to meet with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to discuss an accelerated filing strategy and advance preparations for a Biologics License Application submission for GPS in the first half of 2027.

Comprehensive statistical evaluation of all secondary endpoints and additional pre-specified analyses is underway and will be presented at an upcoming medical conference and submitted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal.

articles.title: China, Russia’s reality check for Trump: Why US sanctions may not matter any more
articles.summary: For a long time, secondary sanctions have served to be an effective tool for the US.
articles.body: For a long time, secondary sanctions have served to be an effective tool for the US. The Donald Trump administration has been aggressively using them in a bid to exercise geoeconomic influence over individuals, businesses and banks linked to countries that it considers as adversaries.In fact, for many years, these measures have proved to be highly effective tools of economic pressure. From the 1980s to the 2010s, the US increasingly used secondary sanctions to transform the dollar-based financial system into a powerful instrument for exerting geopolitical pressure and isolating foreign governments and companies.But that seems to be changing now. Tariffs, secondary sanctions and more - the Donald Trump administration has all tried several tricks up its sleeve to browbeat the global economy. But, the world has survived.A recent report by Henrich Foundation notes: “Overwhelming US sanctions power was for many years a strategic substitute for US military power projection, allowing the economic containment of rival states and thereby freeing up military resources for prime theaters such as the Middle East and East Asia.Also check: 'Hatred stops them from expressing love': Rahul Gandhi slams BJP's reaction on his 'Mumma in Papa's lap' remark, shares photo“In both these regions, however, US military power and sanctions power now appear less capable of deterrence than before,” it says.What has changed? Why is the world less affected by US sanctions and what does this mean for India?How the US built its sanctions powerFor decades, the United States relied on its overwhelming ability to impose sanctions as an alternative to projecting military power. Economic restrictions helped Washington contain rival states while allowing it to reserve military resources for strategically important regions, particularly the Middle East and East Asia.Whether it was the 2000s or 2010s, the US used secondary sanctions to compel European banks to comply with restrictions that were targeted at Iran, Sudan and Cuba.It all started with the growing strength of the dollar as part of the integrated global trading system from the 1980s onwards. This raised the economic cost for countries of being cut off from the US dollar system.According to the Henrich Foundation report, “The traded goods share of global GDP rose continuously from 36% of global GDP in 1979 to 55% of global GDP in 2015.”By the late 1990s and the 2000s, the dollar had firmly established itself not just as the world's leading reserve currency, but also an important invoicing currency, borrowing currency, source of liquidity and vehicle currency for foreign investment.The United States also benefited from a substantial imbalance in economic power. Its position gave it a significant advantage over countries targeted by sanctions, which had relatively few options to retaliate against Washington's economic measures.A further factor underpinning US sanctions’ power was the period of relative macroeconomic stability that lasted from the mid-1980s until the mid-2010s.According to Henrich, from 2010 onward, a fourth pillar further enhanced the US ability to target the main commodity export of its rivals: oil production.“Thanks to easy financing conditions, the US experienced a domestic shale oil boom and became a net exporter of fossil fuels,” its report says.Diminshing impact of US sanctions powerFundamentally, as the risk of sanctions has become more persistent, countries have grown increasingly interested in protecting themselves against their exposure to the US dollar.The Henrich report notes since 2017, and particularly after the “Liberation Day” tariffs that were introduced in spring 2025, US tariff measures have prompted changes in the configuration of global supply chains.“The growing use of export controls on all kinds of strategic items - semiconductors and chipmaking equipment, AI technology, rare earths, and so on - is driving companies and governments to invest in domestic production capacity and in stronger alliance networks that can secure these technologies,” the report says.“On the whole, the world economy has weathered the impact of trade conflict and economic warfare,” it adds.In fact, the report cautions that recent economic research indicates that these developments may weaken US power more severely and more quickly than measures of its overall control over global networks might imply.One of the biggest examples of the diminishing power of America’s secondary sanctions is the strong shadow tanker fleet that continues to globally transport Russian energy supplies.US sanctions against Iran and Venezuela during the 2010s, followed by the coordinated G7 measures against Russia in the early 2020s, progressively excluded several major oil-producing countries from the unrestricted international market centred on the Brent crude benchmark.However, these restrictions did not eliminate the trade in oil. Instead, they redirected it towards alternative channels that are harder to monitor. The global oil market has, in effect, split into two segments: a largely unrestricted market accounting for most oil traded internationally, and a smaller but still substantial “shadow” market created by sanctions.“To supply the growing shadow market in oil, an entire ecosystem of tankers, shipping companies, and insurers formed. Many of this network’s participants function to facilitate the joint trade of Venezuela, Iran, and Russia, while supplying oil importers such as China, India, Türkiye, Vietnam, Indonesia, and others,” the report says.“Despite voluminous and regular new sanctions designations on these ships, companies, and facilitators, secondary sanctions have not proven capable of meaningfully reducing or permanently denting this gray oil market,” the report adds.Not only that, Russia is actively exploring the Northern Sea Route for its exports.And then come China and Iran.China’s restrictions on rare earth exports, alongside Iran’s capacity to disrupt shipping in the Gulf and interfere with oil and gas production in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, have given these countries economic tools with which to push back directly against the US.“This development was apparent in October 2025, when a Chinese embargo on its rare earth exports forced Donald Trump to accept a tariff truce in the Sino-US trade war. Faced with growing shortages in US manufacturing and the defense industry, Trump agreed at an important meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at Busan in South Korea not to impose new export controls and to revert several recent controls on chip exports to China,’ the report explains.Caught off guard by US sanctions targeting its telecommunications sector and chipmakers in 2018–2019, Beijing has spent considerable effort developing a strategy to retaliate with economic pressure during Donald Trump’s second term. Since then, China has further expanded its permanent export-control machinery, ensuring that it can keep this option available for use whenever necessary.“Any significant new US export controls and tariffs risk reactivating a painful Chinese response. But because this stability rests on a commitment to US abstinence from serious secondary sanctions against Chinese entities, Washington’s freedom of maneuver in this space is reduced in the long run,” the report says.Iran, too, has demonstrated its capacity to affect the US economy in 2026. The impact is less immediate and operates through indirect channels, but restrictions on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have triggered a global fuel crisis with consequences for the American economy.Despite being a major exporter of fossil fuels, the US remains vulnerable to oil price shocks in particular product markets.Iran’s strategic position in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with Russia’s natural gas exports, gives the two countries control over approximately 42% of the global natural gas market, covering both liquefied natural gas and supplies transported through pipelines.What this means for USChina, Iran and Russia have built up countervailing economic leverage across a range of critical resources, from rare earth metals to natural gas and petroleum products. Although these capabilities do not eliminate the considerable geoeconomic power that the US Treasury retains through secondary sanctions, they have made it harder for Washington to deploy economic coercion without facing resistance.Yet another important point to note is that the effects of US sanctions are increasingly being felt in the Treasury market as foreign governments are reducing their exposure to US debt.The report points out that foreign official holdings fell 8.4% from $4.24 trillion in January 2021 to $3.87 trillion in December 2025, while China has more than halved its holdings over the past decade. This has given Beijing greater scope to use Treasury sales to pressure Washington.The trend accelerated after the US attack on Iran, with overseas public-sector holdings dropping 6.3% between February and August 2026, including a 31% fall in short-term Treasury bills to $312 billion.What it means for IndiaFor India, the news is mixed. Sanctions are seen as an economic leverage, but India has till now not finalised a trade deal with the US, insisting on a competitive advantage. It has also not stopped buying Russian crude. Resilience in exports through diversified markets and trade agreements has also helped in India.According to Vivek Iyer, Partner and Financial Services Risk Advisory Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat, India is moderately exposed to sanctions pressure, and in a few concentrated areas.“The thesis that alternative networks blunt sanctions mostly helps countries that are themselves sanctioned, like Russia and Iran. India is a third country. Its banks, exporters and refiners rely heavily on dollar clearing and US markets, so a secondary-sanctions threat still works on India even if it has weakened against Russia,” he tells TOI.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Energy remains the biggest exposure. The new Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act allows the US to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas. India, which takes more Russian crude than any country except China, is one of them.On October 16, Trump waived sections 112 and 113 and most of the Act's sanctions provisions, but that waiver is discretionary and can be reversed. Russia's share of India's crude imports was roughly 56% at its height and fell to about 35% in September.And there is a past precedent to US pressure when Trump imposed a 25% penal tariff on India for its Russian oil purchases. India did not stop buying Russian crude oil due to tariffs, but subsequent sanctions on Russian oil majors did force it to recalibrate oil procurement strategy.Yet, the US needs India both strategically and in oil markets.Ajay Srivastava, founder, Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) believes that India remains vulnerable at both the company and country levels.“The risk has already shaped India’s energy choices. India stopped buying Iranian crude and previously cut back on Venezuelan oil to avoid US sanctions. articles.title: Rs 20-60 lakh humanoids turn heads at Bengaluru Tech Summit
articles.summary: Humanoid robots priced Rs 20–60 lakh drew crowds at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 as Unitree showcased G1 and robotic dogs for research and industry.

Initially known for its relatively affordable robotic dogs, the company has expanded into humanoid robots capable of walking, running and performing complex movements. It competes in a growing market that includes Tesla and Boston Dynamics.Unitree made its stock market debut in Shanghai in August this year, raising about $904 million.At the summit, the company displayed its G1 humanoid, which is used for research and development, object handling and navigation. A representative at the stall said about 50 humanoid units had been sold in India, including to large companies, though he declined to identify the buyers.The G1 is priced between Rs 20 lakh and Rs 60 lakh in India, depending on its configuration and application, the representative said. The robot can handle objects weighing around 2-3 kg.Unitree also displayed its quadruped robotic dog, used by universities and research institutions. The representative said the company’s other models included robots designed for firefighting and a G1-D humanoid intended for logistics and warehousing applications.While humanoid robots are attracting growing interest globally, commercial deployment remains limited, with much of the current demand coming from research, education and demonstrations.Money habits form by age 7. articles.summary: General Autonomy’s quadruped robot Param won the first robot race at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, reaching 4.3 m/s as Indian firms showcased autonomous robots.

The event brought together Indian robotics companies to showcase advances in physical AI and autonomous machines.The race involved robots completing a lap of a designated track, with the fastest to return to the starting line declared the winner. Incubated at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in partnership with the defence sector, M3 was initially developed for defence applications and is now being adapted for industrial surveillance, construction sites and safety and security operations.One of M3’s distinguishing features is its payload capacity of about 45 kg, higher than that of Xterra’s Dhav, though the latter’s newer models offer comparable capacity.The demonstrations highlighted how Indian robotics firms are developing machines for applications beyond controlled factory environments, including defence, infrastructure and industrial operations.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Why Is Micron Stock Down Nearly 8%?
articles.summary: Today's big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash.
articles.body:
Shares of Micron Technology (MU) dropped 7.6% on Monday, November 16, 2026, as the S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The company released no announcements, earnings reports or filings. But 33 of the 34 other semiconductor companies worth $2 billion or more also fell that day. So what pulled chip stocks lower on Monday, and how is Micron tied to it?

Chip Stocks Slid Ahead Of Two Tests For AI

Chip stocks fell on November 16 ahead of two tests for the AI trade. The first is Nvidia's results, due Tuesday. The second is Anthropic's expected trading debut on Thursday. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.5% the same day.

Micron's business is closely tied to the AI trade. AI data centers are using memory faster than manufacturers can produce it, pushing memory prices higher. Micron's revenue and profit have grown on AI data center demand. Revenue reached $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter ended September 3, up 379.3% from a year earlier.

On its September 30 call, management said it expected margins for the rest of fiscal 2027 to be wider than in fiscal Q1 2027. It said continued price increases, at a more moderate pace, would help.

Did Micron Fall More Than Other Chip Makers?

Yes. Micron fell more than the typical company in its semiconductor sub-industry. The median drop among the 34 other companies was 5.1%. Eighteen of them fell 5% or more. Only one of them rose. XLK, a fund that tracks the technology sector, lost 3.2%. Every company on Micron's peer list fell too, including Intel, down 7.0%, and Western Digital, down 5.0%.

Where Micron Stock Stands After A Weak Month

A fall this large is not rare for Micron. The stock had 12 such falls in the prior 365 days. Its most recent move at least this large in either direction came on November 11, when it rose 11.9% in a single session. Over the past twelve months, Micron returned 203.8%, against 11.4% for the S&P 500. From October 16 to November 16, the stock went the other way, down 18.2% while the index lost 3.1%.

Micron closed at $719.02 on November 16. That is well below its highest close of the past year, $1,213.56 on June 25, 2026. Its lowest close in that time was $201.37 on November 20, 2025. The stock trades at 6.1 times its sales over the past twelve months, against 3.2 times for the S&P 500.

Micron is expected to report its fiscal Q1 2027 results in December 2026. Its gross margin, 86.8% in fiscal Q4 2026, is the measure to watch in that report.

Micron itself announced nothing on Monday, and the stock still dropped with nearly every chip maker.

articles.title: Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate?
articles.summary: A rift has emerged in Trump’s cabinet over China’s access to advanced AI chips as export controls tighten.
articles.body:
A rift between United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over sales of advanced computer chips to China has spilled into public view.

On Monday, the administration of President Donald Trump introduced new rules requiring licences to sell advanced chips to buyers in named third countries suspected of being conduits to China. The new restrictions were written by Bessent’s Department of the Treasury and the White House – not Lutnick’s Department of Commerce, which usually oversees chip exports.

Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, has so far not taken a side.

As the US reels from the resignation of chip maker Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang last week over revelations that he had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, here’s what this all means.

The two cabinet members, who are both veteran investors, disagree over how strictly the US should limit China’s access to the advanced chips that power artificial intelligence (AI).

The US restricts exports of certain advanced AI chips to China. In December 2025, Trump announced that Nvidia could sell its H200 chip to approved Chinese customers, on condition that 25 percent of the revenue would go to the US government. In January, the administration relaxed licensing rules for the H200 and similar chips.

On Monday, new controls were issued to monitor access to US chips in Southeast Asia and Brazil – penned by Bessent with the backing of the National Security Council, not by Lutnick.

As commerce secretary, Lutnick oversees these export controls and is charged with determining which critical technologies US companies can sell abroad, with an eye towards national security.

He has been one of the administration’s most vocal supporters of allowing Nvidia, the world’s dominant maker of AI super chips, to sell to China, despite the fact that it is racing against the US to dominate development of the AI industry.

“You want to sell the Chinese enough that their developers get addicted to the American technology stack,” Lutnick said in July 2025.

But US rules still bar the most advanced chips from being sold to China, and reports of restricted Nvidia chips allegedly being smuggled into the country through unofficial routes have put Lutnick’s role under the microscope.

Lutnick’s department was accused of turning a blind eye to such smuggling and stalling a planned crackdown on actors thought to be involved.

Fellow cabinet members and lawmakers have questioned his department’s handling of the issue, and some lawmakers say it has undermined US national security.

Bessent has pressed for tougher enforcement of existing export rules.

“We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented,” he said on Friday.

The two men have been rivals for some time. In 2024, Elon Musk and other Trump allies lobbied for Lutnick to get the Treasury job, but it ultimately went to Bessent.

Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for the most advanced chips used for AI. Worth trillions of dollars, it is among the world’s most valuable companies, and its customers include tech giants Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta.

Nvidia’s cofounder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, whom some US officials have suspected of working for Chinese intelligence – a claim denied by China.

Alice Huang is a former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that builds data centres in Southeast Asia which cater for Chinese clients.

Megaspeed bought more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips in about two years, but US authorities suspect that many of these chips were then smuggled into China rather than used in Megaspeed’s data centres, a charge it denies.

On Friday, Bessent said four government agencies, including the Treasury, had pushed for months to put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, but Lutnick’s Commerce Department had not acted.

“Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

He also questioned whether Nvidia had properly vetted its customers.

“The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said.

The new rules require companies to obtain a US licence before shipping advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries Washington suspects of acting as conduit routes for chips to reach China.

It also requires any data centre in the world using Nvidia chips to obtain Washington’s permission before it can “rent” computer power to Chinese customers. This closes a loophole that previously allowed Chinese companies to “rent” the use of advanced chips without purchasing them outright.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the restrictions as “economic coercion” and said Beijing would take “necessary measures” in response.

In Washington, the new restrictions were welcomed by John Moolenaar, the Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China.

The committee, a panel of lawmakers focused on competition with China’s ruling Communist Party, is one of the most hawkish voices on Beijing in Congress. Moolenaar criticised the administration’s decision last year to ease curbs on Nvidia’s chip sales to China.

“Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy,” he said.

Senior officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have argued for keeping the most advanced chips out of China, while lawmakers from both parties have criticised Lutnick.

“It would be dumb and stupid for us to sell that to anybody, especially a country that’s going to reverse-engineer it and leapfrog us,” Rubio said in May.

Greer made a similar case last week, saying that US “crown jewels” should remain in US hands or in the hands of allies.

David Sacks, Trump’s former AI adviser, however, defended selling chips to China and dismissed those pushing for tighter controls.

“The policy of the China hawks is effectively the policy of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party]. Neither one wants American chips in China,” he said in a podcast appearance on Saturday.

On the other side of the political aisle, some Democrats have called for Lutnick to step down from his position for his failure to police chip smuggling.

“Making powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security and economic competitiveness,” Senator Richard Blumenthal said in a post on X.

Both Lutnick and Jensen Huang have been summoned to testify before the Senate on December 3.

Trump has swung between restricting and allowing Nvidia’s sales to China. In April 2025, the White House curbed sales of the H20, a chip Nvidia made for the Chinese market – only to agree to allow them three months later.

His later decision in December to permit sales of the more powerful H200 marked a further easing of those restrictions.

Trump has stood by Lutnick, saying on Monday that he was not planning to remove him, days after the Reuters news agency reported that top White House aides had debated whether he should go.

Trump has acknowledged that the issue is splitting his cabinet, without explicitly taking sides.

“It’s a different viewpoint. One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Trump said. “They both are acceptable, but they are different views.”

Trump has also said it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia .

Trump and Xi are due to meet in Shenzhen on Thursday, during this week’s APEC summit. Ahead of their last meeting , when Xi visited the US in September, Washington banned imports of Chinese-made humanoid robots and threatened to sanction Chinese AI firms.
